assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and have redefined what a precision instrument can do. They enable tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and a path to a redefinition of the second. This is exactly the kind of new measurement technique that creates a fresh observational window, with systematics treated carefully, which I value as an instrument builder.
assessment.attribution: The credited list is a clean pair. Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and demonstrated early Sr clocks. Ye's group pushed the performance to the extreme and broadened the applications. Related single-ion clock and comb work was recognized earlier (2005, 2012), so the citation would need care to separate it from prior prizes.
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent labs (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and others) have confirmed and compared clocks well below 1e-17. The technology is mature and the interpretation stable, and the timing is good given that a redefinition of the second is being prepared.
uncertainties: Overlap with the earlier 2005 and 2012 AMO prizes could be seen as incremental by some members.
I cannot verify from the supplied text whether other early proposers of lattice clocks deserve credit.
This is outside my own specialty, so I would rely on AMO colleagues for finer attribution.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: IceCube turned a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice into a neutrino telescope, established a diffuse flux of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos, and then pointed to the blazar TXS 0506+056 and the Galactic plane as sources. That is a genuine new window on the high-energy universe, achieved through a very demanding detector project. As an astroparticle physicist I rate it highly for originality, difficulty and lasting impact.
assessment.attribution: A large collaboration, so credit is intrinsically difficult. Halzen is the long-time leader and visionary of the project. Karle is the detector-building physicist among the supplied names. Shigeru Yoshida is another plausible name, so a two- or three-person split can be defended. The decisive contribution is the observatory itself and the 2013 discovery of the flux.
assessment.maturity: The diffuse flux is confirmed by independent IceCube analyses and, at lower significance, by ANTARES and Baikal-GVD. The TXS 0506+056 association is at about 3 sigma, and the NGC 1068 and Galactic plane results are newer, though the discovery of the flux itself is robust. Timing is reasonable while the field is still developing.
uncertainties: Source identification beyond a few objects is still limited.
Allocation among IceCube founders and leaders may be contested, and the supplied names may not capture all decisive people.
Some members may see overlap with the 2002 prize for cosmic neutrino detection.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The discovery of X-ray and optical afterglows of gamma-ray bursts settled a thirty-year puzzle by placing the bursts at cosmological distances, and it launched modern transient and multi-messenger astrophysics. The result rested on the BeppoSAX instrument and a rapid localisation chain, which appeals strongly to me. The impact is large and lasting.
assessment.attribution: Costa and Frontera led the BeppoSAX gamma-ray burst monitor and wide-field cameras that gave arc-minute positions. Kulkarni's group provided optical and radio afterglow and redshift follow-up. Other essential contributors, such as the optical discoverers and spectroscopists, are not in the supplied list, and the credit configuration is the main weakness. The three listed names can support a configuration, but not without argument.
assessment.maturity: The discovery is very well confirmed by Swift, HETE-2, Fermi and thousands of later afterglows, and the cosmological origin and connections to supernovae and kilonovae are firmly settled. It is a mature result, and timing matters given the ages of the protagonists.
uncertainties: Attribution is the principal risk, since some essential contributors are missing from the list and at least one key person may be deceased (not verified).
Whether the citation should recognise the instrument or the physics of the origin is open.
Colleagues may weigh the instrument-versus-astrophysics balance differently from me.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, followed by the HgTe observation, created a major field of topological quantum matter with lasting conceptual impact. Theory and experiment are both original, and the subject has changed how condensed-matter physics is organised.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele are the theoretical originators of the Z2 classification and the spin-orbit quantum spin Hall proposal. Molenkamp led the HgTe quantum well experiment that realised the effect. Hasan's work on three-dimensional materials is another strong claim, but the three-name limit forces a choice, and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal is not among the supplied names, which is an unresolved question.
assessment.maturity: The effect is confirmed in several materials by independent groups, and the interpretation is stable. The topological paradigm was recognised in 2016 with a related prize, so some will see this as a sequel, but the field is now mature.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2016 prize for topological phase transitions.
The roles of Hasan and of the HgTe theory proposers in the allocation of credit.
Condensed matter is outside my expertise, so I rely on colleagues.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance in magnetic tunnel junctions, and later the MgO coherent-tunnelling enhancement, enabled magnetic read heads and MRAM. It is a clear case of solid-state spin transport that became a technology in billions of devices, and the practical use is concrete and unambiguous.
assessment.attribution: Miyazaki and Moodera independently reported large room-temperature TMR in 1995, a good example of a joint discovery. Parkin demonstrated the MgO-based large effect and led the industrial route. Others, who are not among the supplied names, also contributed to the MgO result.
assessment.maturity: The effect has been confirmed many times and underpins an industry. It followed the 2007 GMR prize, so timing is mature, though some may view it as a continuation.
uncertainties: Relationship to the 2007 GMR prize may reduce its perceived novelty.
The MgO contribution by other groups complicates the attribution.
I rely on condensed-matter colleagues to judge the physics novelty.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Baryon acoustic oscillations give a standard ruler that is a robust probe of cosmic expansion and dark energy. Detecting the feature required very large survey instruments (SDSS and 2dF), and the result now underpins DESI and Euclid. It is an important and lasting cosmological measurement.
assessment.attribution: Eisenstein and collaborators made the SDSS detection in 2005, and Cole and the 2dFGRS team the contemporaneous one. Sunyaev contributed to the early theoretical prediction of acoustic features, as did others not on the supplied list. Credit is broad and the survey teams are large, so the configuration is arguable.
assessment.maturity: The detection is confirmed in many surveys (BOSS, eBOSS, WiggleZ, DESI) and the ruler is a standard tool. Recent DESI hints of evolving dark energy are unsettled but do not undermine the detection itself.
uncertainties: Prediction credit involves people who are not on the supplied list.
Large survey collaborations make personal credit difficult to assign.
Cosmology of this kind is partly outside my own specialty.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry has turned matter-wave interference into a precision instrument for measuring gravity, rotation and fundamental constants, with applications in inertial navigation and tests of general relativity. It is a technique-driven field with a clear instrument legacy, which suits my own criteria.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard, Bordé and Kasevich each made decisive early contributions (early atom interferometers, the Ramsey-Bordé interferometer, light-pulse gravimeters and gyroscopes). Others outside the supplied list also contributed, so a fair three-person configuration is arguable but not obvious.
assessment.maturity: The method is replicated at many labs and commercial gravimeters exist, so the field is mature. Large-scale fundamental-physics applications are still developing, so recognition could be judged slightly early or late depending on viewpoint.
uncertainties: Overlap with earlier cooling and trapping prizes.
Priority among the credited names and others is not obviously settled.
Atomic physics lies outside my expertise.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The evidence for a nanohertz gravitational-wave background from pulsar timing arrays opens an entirely new band, and timing millisecond pulsars to tens of nanoseconds is an impressive precision technique. If the signal is confirmed as arising from supermassive black hole binaries, it would be prize-worthy.
assessment.attribution: The result comes from the NANOGrav, EPTA, PPTA and CPTA collaborations. Manchester led the Parkes effort, Kramer the European one and McLaughlin is a NANOGrav leader. The listed trio reflects leaders, but credit among many collaborators and earlier method proposals is uncertain.
assessment.maturity: The Hellings-Downs-like correlation is at a few sigma in each array and the datasets are broadly consistent, but a combined high-significance detection and identification of the source are still to come. I would regard recognition as premature at present.
uncertainties: Statistical significance is below the conventional discovery threshold in individual arrays, as I recall it.
The astrophysical origin (black hole binaries versus new physics) is unresolved.
Credit is spread across several collaborations and decades of method development.
